discrete

/dih-SKREET/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Discrete means individually separate and distinct — made of clearly divided parts rather than one continuous whole.

The bridge project was planned as four discrete stages, each with its own budget, crew, and deadline.

Example

The questionnaire sorts ages into discrete categories — under 18, 18 to 34, 35 to 64, and 65 and up — with no overlap between them.

The age brackets are separate, non-overlapping units with clean boundaries between them. That clear division into distinct parts is exactly what discrete captures.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

distinct: Distinct means clearly different and individual — each voice in the choir was distinct. Discrete adds a structural claim: the parts are cleanly divided units with no overlap or blending between them. Two flavors can be distinct while swirled together in one scoop; discrete scoops sit in separate bowls.

self-contained: Self-contained means complete in itself — a self-contained apartment has its own kitchen and bath, needing nothing outside itself. Discrete claims only clean separation between parts of a larger whole: a book's chapters are discrete, yet not one of them stands complete on its own.

standalone: Standalone describes something that works entirely on its own, unattached to any larger system — a standalone film needs no sequels. Discrete parts, by contrast, still belong to one whole; they are simply divided cleanly from one another, like the numbered stages of a single project.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

continuous: unbroken; without divisions

merged: combined into one

Where it sits · how completely apart something stands

separate → discrete → isolated

separate vs. discrete: Separate is the milder, everyday word: two separate rooms can still share a door, while discrete parts stand fully apart as clearly divided units.

isolated vs. discrete: Isolated is stronger than discrete: an isolated outpost is not just a distinct unit — it is cut off from everything around it, which discrete never implies.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — dis-: apart

Root — cret: sifted, separated (Latin cernere, cretus — to sift, to distinguish)

Put it together: From Latin discretus, "sifted apart": dis- (apart) + cretus (sifted, separated) — like grain sifted into clearly separate piles, each part distinct from the rest.

Use the root in a new word: discerning: The discerning editor set three manuscripts aside before lunch and never glanced at them again.

Root Check

Word Choice

Academic / technical

Spelling is everything here: discrete (-crete) means separate and distinct — discrete steps, discrete categories, discrete units. Discreet (-eet) is a different word entirely in modern English: it means careful and tactful about what you reveal. Data comes in discrete units; a friend who keeps your news quiet is being discreet. Quick test: if you can swap in "separate," the word you want is discrete.
